articles.title: No, Digger Is Not a Misunderstood Masterpiece
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: You may have heard already that Digger , the new film cowritten and directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu ( The Revenant, Birdman ) and starring Tom Cruise, is an expensive box-office bomb that got many annihilating reviews . One of the better ones sums it up perfectly: “It’s like being trapped inside a tuba for two hours.” Bad news travels fast. And I’m going to further speed it along by providing an all-spoiler review, so consider yourself warned. This is in order to convince you that you’d be better off staying home watching Dr. Strangelove , Stanley Kubrick’s scathingly funny and incisive 1964 protest against world-ending insanity, which set the template for satirical black comedy for generations to come. Cue the predictable guardians of art and high culture emerging to defend Digger from us lowbrow proles who can’t appreciate cinematic brilliance and originality when they see it. See bits of it in previews, that is. They’re not crazy enough to actually go see the whole gruelingly unfunny and uninvolving movie. Very few people are, besides all the embittered film critics obligated to see Digger , sitting there alone in vast dark theaters trying to come up with new adjectives to describe their own jaded disaffection. As happens much more frequently than is generally acknowledged when it comes to films, the lowbrow proles are right. Digger is dead on arrival. All that big-budget prestige-picture money, all that great acting talent (John Goodman, Riz Ahmed, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg, Jesse Plemons), all that lushly beautiful cinematography (Emmanuel Lubezki) and production design (Dennis Gassner and Richard L. Johnson), all that topical relevance, and for what? So you can watch Tom Cruise, nearly unrecognizable in gray hair, old-age makeup and prosthetics, and a fake potbelly, stomping around braying his lines as the title character Digger Rockwell, a crazily overconfident Texas oil tycoon tasked with preventing the ultimate world-destroying climate catastrophe that his own massive oil-drilling company created. The Big Meta “Twist” Falls Flat Signing big star Tom Cruise presumably got Iñárritu that extravagant reported budget of $125 million to make what amounts to a ponderous art film. You know the kind of art film I mean, the one that reveals partway through that all the characters shouting and crying and vomiting and making faces all over the place are in fact actors performing roles in a play — which is the big twist in Digger . At a certain point, Tom Cruise even stops hollering in an overripe, hog-calling Texas accent and speaks in his own voice in order to complain to the play’s director that he finds the Digger character “cartoonish” and feels “disconnected” from him and the whole experience. If this film weren’t so enervating, that would be the moment to yell at the screen, “You and me both, Tommy boy!” But no one’s got that kind of energy, not when the camera is heading backstage to show us that this is all actually a production of a theatrical cult hit called Fossil Fools . It seems the survivors of horrific climate catastrophes that occurred in the real world and wiped out much of the human population find it cathartic to watch those disasters replayed onstage, along with the downfall of Digger. It’s not that everyone involved in the production — the Digger production, I mean, not the Fossil Fools production — isn’t trying hard to sell the material. Part of the misery of watching it is seeing all the actors struggling to put their undeveloped characters across in wearying scenes full of rotten dialogue. Tom Cruise is generally effortful and a bit exhausting anyway — it’s part of his star persona — but as Digger he wears you out a quarter of the way into the film. Then there are the fabulous actors in supporting roles giving their all. John Goodman plays President Compson, another loud idiot, who’s grappling with the world-ending scenario created by Digger while suffering from “a-s cancer.” It’s a deadly affliction which will turn out to be convenient because he’ll be safely under the knife at Walter Reed Hospital when someone has to answer for the recent massive catastrophe. The subservient vice president, called “Eddie” throughout and played by Michael Stuhlbarg ( A Serious Man ), is deputized to face the enraged governing body. Meanwhile, Dr Nirav Ganesh (Riz Ahmed of Four Lions and Nightcrawler ), the earnest scientist who heads Digger’s environmental safety team, tries in vain to get any of the blowhards in charge to listen to him before it’s too late. An Astonishing Waste of Talent Other phenomenal actors are entirely wasted in nothing roles. Sandra Hüller, who came to international prominence in Anatomy of a Fall and The Zone of Interest , plays a few scenes as Emma, Digger’s much younger, cluelessly self-centered half-sister and business partner who’s allowed to run a company dedicated to clean energy that Digger treats as a joke. Jesse Plemons roams into scenes in the framing narrative about putting on the play, because he’s portraying Kenny Rockwell, Digger’s nephew, who owns the rights to the play Fossil Fools and encourages the cast to carry on mocking his ridiculous destroyer-of-worlds family because it’s cathartic for the play’s audiences. Burn Gorman, an excellent English character actor whom you’ll recognize if you’re a BritBox subscriber, literally has no lines and only one bit of business — an absurdly overdone patriotic salute when President Compson launches nuclear weapons at the massive ice shelf that broke off from Greenland and is about to crash into the western coast of the European continent, causing massive damage and loss of life. Nuking things, always the recommendation of military brass, only creates more problems, however. Featured in many more scenes and frankly performed with greater care is an animatronic white cat named Maggie, the only creature that Digger loves. She’s thirty years old and dying of several fatal conditions, a pitiable creature cruelly kept alive by the moronically doting Digger. That’s all played for laughs, by the way, just to give you a sense of Iñárritu’s comic stylings. It’s depressing to read about the ten-year development of this film involving writer-director Iñárritu and star-producer Tom Cruise. Iñárritu says the “spine” of the project was always Digger’s long monologue delivered to the European Parliament midway through the film, in which Digger admits to all charges against him about enriching himself through endless oil drilling and environmental despoliation, and covering up studies that would’ve provided proof for scientists trying to awaken the public to the dangers of fossil fuel reliance. Digger then proceeds to blame all the ordinary people in the world for this. He keeps the oil pumping because we all selfishly want to heat and cool our homes and drive cars and have cell phones. According to Iñárritu, he gave Digger ultimate persuasive power in this central scene because, as he puts it, “I’m not interested in pointing fingers or reducing the film to a political commentary or a right or left thing.” For Iñárritu, “we are all part of this madness.” It’s with a weary sense of inevitability that we watch this scene, which shifts blame to the struggling masses just trying to get by in a world run by vicious self-serving plutocrats. It doesn’t even make sense in terms of the rest of the film, which is dedicated to mocking the monstrous venality and cluelessness of billionaires and the politicians who serve them. Nevertheless, Iñárritu still wants to know if all of us relatively powerless people are now ready to dig deep and sacrifice any creature comforts we might have in order to save the world. For him, it’s all in our power to do it somehow. At the end of the film, the audiences shown flocking to see Fossil Fools to gloat over Digger’s demise are all wrong, failing to learn the proper lesson from the ongoing apocalypse — that “there are no good or bad people” and we all have to work together, kumbaya. This is a message that might have been convincing in the early 2010s. In 2026, with plenty of genuinely very bad people at the top of both our government and our economy — people who seem to even embrace their villainous powers — it falls very, very flat. articles.title: Lula Is in Danger of Losing Brazil’s Presidency
articles.author: Aldo Cordeiro Sauda
articles.content: The first round of Brazil’s elections dealt a heavy blow to the Workers’ Party (PT) and, more broadly, to the cause of democracy in Latin America. In 2022, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva finished some six million votes ahead of Jair Bolsonaro in the first round, a margin that narrowed to about two million in the runoff. This time, Flávio Bolsonaro finished 2.2 million votes ahead of Lula, a lead of three percentage points. That makes the second round on October 25 especially difficult for Lula and the Brazilian left. The candidates who finished behind the top two, who together took around six million votes (roughly 6 percent), are all on the far right. They supported Jair Bolsonaro’s government and opposed Lula’s, so a broad front is likely to form against him in the runoff. There is a real chance that the Bolsonaro family will return to the presidency. Right-Wing Momentum The same dynamic shaped the legislative races. In the Senate, Bolsonaro’s far-right Liberal Party (PL) grew from fifteen seats to twenty-eight, while the PT held steady at nine (out of eighty-one in total). Hopes for a larger female presence in Congress also went unrealized. The gubernatorial races told a similar story. Sergio Moro, the far-right senator who jailed Lula in the wake of the parliamentary and judicial coup against Dilma Rousseff, won the governorship of Paraná in the first round. The far right also won outright in wealthy states like Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul. In the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil’s lower house, the PT fared especially badly in São Paulo state, where veteran party figures such as Paulo Teixeira, Nabil Bonduki, and José Dirceu failed to win seats. The PT’s top candidate in the state, Luana Zaratini, received 230,000 votes, while the PL’s top candidate, Luciano Pavanato, received three million. Nationally, the left-wing parties with parliamentary representation — the PT, the Party of Socialism and Liberty, Rede, and the Communist Party — grew from eighty-eight deputies to ninety-six. But they were outpaced by Bolsonaro’s PL, which jumped from ninety-nine to 120 (out of 513 in total). When Bolsonaro was first elected, in 2018, the general mood was one of revolt. The far right rode into office on an enthusiastic movement from below, one that filled the streets. This has not happened with Flávio this year. Despite the PL’s electoral success and the strength of Bolsonarismo in the ballot box, the streets are lukewarm. The promises sound less like a plan to overturn everything, as in the previous campaign, and more like one to resume the Right’s unfinished work, especially amnesty for the family and revenge against the Supreme Court. The movement now coming from above might be more dangerous than the one coming from below. American Interference Contrary to expectations, US intervention did not take the form of noisy meddling by Donald Trump and his allies. It appears to have come instead through effective background pressure on the Federal Police and the Supreme Court, which became the center of the political debate. This proved particularly damaging. Rather than debating questions of policy and program, the campaign revolved around corruption, the far right’s favorite terrain. And this time, the debate centered more on the Supreme Court than on the presidency. The first thing Washington did after Jair Bolsonaro’s arrest was to apply the Magnitsky Act, imposing sanctions on the magistrate responsible for the case, Alexandre de Moraes, to punish him for going after Trump’s main ally on the continent. The pressure on the Brazilian judicial system has continued ever since, less visibly but with greater aggression. The court’s own conduct made it an easy target. Its justices have a record of protecting bourgeois interests, and the line between public and private affairs is poorly drawn: justices commonly become multimillionaire lawyers once they leave the bench. This is the story of the Banco Master scandal. Judges and, above all, their relatives were tied to multimillion-dollar contracts, favors, gifts, and Epstein-style parties organized by the fraudulent banker at the center of the biggest financial crime in Brazil’s history. Among them was Moraes’s wife, Viviane Moraes. Five of the court’s eleven justices were implicated, yet the crisis revolved around Moraes, and the far right used it to attack the figure who had put Bolsonaro behind bars. The key question about the revelation of Viviane Moraes’s secret deals is how Justice André Mendonça, a far-right evangelical preacher with close ties to the US evangelical right, got access to the confidential documents. The manner, the speed, and the access enjoyed by this Bolsonaro appointee strongly suggest that there was US interference in the process. During a heated Supreme Court session broadcast live on television one month before the vote, Moraes said the report had been drafted in a time frame of seventy-two hours and insisted that time frame was impossible for a document of that kind. According to him, the metadata proved the report had not been produced by the Federal Police at all but by outside agents, likely foreigners, who simply handed the final product to the police. The metadata, Moraes insisted, showed that the police inquiry was opened and closed on the same day on a Federal Police computer, meaning the report had merely been inserted into it. He described this as evidence of attempted foreign interference in Brazil’s elections. Mendonça also intervened during the offensive against Moraes by ousting the chief of the Federal Police, whom Lula had appointed and who had been responsible for containing the January 8, 2023 coup attempt. Probable US intervention in the controversy over the Supreme Court shifted the terms of the debate to the advantage of the Brazilian right, in contrast with the punitive tariffs Trump imposed after Bolsonaro’s imprisonment that merely increased support for Lula. This time, the focus was not on the action taken by the Trump administration but on the allegations of corruption among judges who had backed the Lula government. A Weak Government While the focus on the Supreme Court certainly made things easier for Bolsonaro, it is impossible to ignore the fact that Lula’s third government has been the least transformative of his three terms. This is partly explained by how Brazil’s institutions have evolved since the coup against his successor, Dilma Rousseff. The coup against Dilma was both a coup by parliament and a coup for parliament. The conservative right in Congress toppled her to install one of its own leading figures, Vice President Michel Temer, in the presidency. At the same time, it also sought to weaken the executive and strengthen the legislature, while the process also empowered the Supreme Court at the presidency’s expense. As a result of these efforts, Lula’s ability to govern has been greatly restricted and depends far more on Congress, including on matters like the budget. Under Bolsonaro, Congress took a direct institutional hand in writing the budget and directing public spending autonomously, in a way never seen before, and that practice has continued under Lula. According to political scientist André Singer, Brazil has moved from a presidential system built on broad parliamentary coalitions to something closer to a semi-presidential postcoup regime. But the weakening of the presidency does not in itself explain why the PT did so poorly. The government has relatively little to show in terms of improving the lives of the working class. It is true that unemployment is lower than ever, while levels of hunger have been reduced to the benchmark of Lula’s earlier governments, after rising sharply under Temer and (especially) Bolsonaro . But while life has largely returned to its pre-pandemic form, conditions remain very hard for working people. In the final Quaest poll before the election, voters in households earning up to twice the minimum wage (about US$620 a month) backed Lula over Flávio by 52 percent to 23 percent. That group has seen life improve as extreme poverty fell after the pandemic. However, this was not enough to offset the PT’s losses elsewhere. Among households earning two to five times the minimum wage, Flávio led narrowly by 36 percent to 35 percent. Among those earning more than five times, he led by a wider margin, 42 percent to 30 percent. While hunger has fallen, food prices have continued to rise, albeit to a lesser extent than under Bolsonaro. The quality of food has declined, with more semi-industrial products and higher prices for meat and other staples that were far more accessible before COVID-19. The availability of meat matters in particular: it played a central role in Lula’s 2022 campaign. Employment tells a similar story. Unemployment is down, but work has become harder. Temer’s administration stripped away a series of labor rights, and none of those rights has been restored under Lula. Jobs under PJ ( pessoa jurídica ) contracts, which cover individual freelancers and sole proprietors, have grown at the expense of formal employment, bringing far greater insecurity. Much of the job growth has come in service sectors tied to apps and digital platforms, where poor conditions and a lack of protections have made life worse. Debt Debt is a particular problem. Working-class indebtedness has grown, and this is especially relevant for the PT and for Lula, because the party’s governmental strategy has been to expand the capacity of families to take on debt. When it came to transport, for example, the main strategy was to widen access to car purchases through credit, rather than invest heavily in public transit. There was a huge expansion of access to housing for those earning one to five times the minimum wage. But almost all of it came from subsidizing private housing through the Minha Casa, Minha Vida program, which widened access by pushing people into debt. Public universities expanded, but the largest growth was in private institutions, through grants and financing schemes that also meant taking on more debt. In other words, the gains of the Lula and Dilma governments rested on greater access to goods like cars, housing, and education, bought with increased household debt. More than two decades after the launch of policies that sought to integrate the working class into mass society through consumption, 80 percent of families now carry high levels of debt. The Left and the Mass Movements Efforts to avoid conflict with Congress, the Supreme Court, and Brazil’s capitalist class also made it harder for Lula’s government to deliver on its campaign pledges. While devastation of the Amazon jungle was reduced, Lula made drilling for oil off the mouth of the Amazon River one of his priorities after taking office, posing a serious risk of spills along the Amazonian coast. His government also announced a plan that would have placed strategic stretches of the Madeira, Tapajós, and Tocantins rivers in the National Privatization Program, with the aim of turning them into export corridors for soybeans. It was mobilization by indigenous and student movements during the COP30 protests in Belém do Pará that stopped the project. The early supporters of this abortive scheme included Guilherme Boulos, the minister in charge of the presidential general secretariat and relations with social movements, and Sônia Guajajara, the minister of indigenous peoples. Guajajara won 160,000 votes in the 2022 elections; this time, she received just 54,000. Most telling was the government’s failure, or unwillingness, to convert workers’ struggles into mobilizations in its favor. The central working-class demand since Lula’s election has been for an end to the 6x1 schedule (six days of work followed by one day off) and a reduction of the working week. However, the PT channeled this demand into a purely parliamentary fight with no strikes or street protests to back it up. The same demobilizing logic applied to the app workers’ strike (the breque dos apps ), perhaps the most explosive moment of working-class struggle in São Paulo during recent years. While the government moved to head off the strike, the only proposal it offered these workers was credit to buy bicycles. Foreign Policy In terms of foreign policy, Lula’s government never developed a coherent line of opposition to the policies of the Trump administration. It did not follow through on threats to directly tax American goods and preferred to negotiate with Washington over its invocation of the Magnitsky Act. In relation to Palestine, Lula did put forward an early condemnation of Israel’s genocide, and his government joined South Africa’s genocide case at the International Court of Justice last year. However, the administration also used the human rights ministry to counterbalance its relationship with Tel Aviv. Silvio de Almeida, the human rights minister who left the post amid sexual harassment allegations, refused for months to condemn the genocide, saying it was a matter for the president and the foreign ministry. His successor, Macaé Evaristo, steered the ministry toward a policy of “combating antisemitism” that involved visiting Jewish institutions, the Holocaust museum, and pro-Zionist synagogues while ignoring the Palestinian community and taking no stand against Islamophobia. The government’s response to the failed Bolsonarist coup was also inadequate. It supported the Supreme Court while it declined to pursue important targets such as the Argentine Fernando Cerimedo , who is linked to US and Israeli interference networks in Latin America and was removed from the attorney general’s final indictment, and Jovem Pan, the major media outlet that called for the coup attempt. Winning the Runoff Lula’s most popular moves in the run-up to the election involved changing his administration’s previous positions on those issues. His government had previously tried only to regulate the growth of online betting, which has hit working-class households hard, football betting above all. Now it moved to ban it altogether. Payments under the Bolsa Família scheme, designed to reduce poverty and extreme hunger, had not been increased to take account of inflation over the previous three years. This changed on the eve of the vote. The government also began investing in public health against obesity by buying treatments such as Mounjaro, having previously failed to do so. These policy shifts boosted support for Lula and may even have prevented Flávio Bolsonaro from winning outright in the first round. If Lula is to be reelected in the runoff, he has to generate hope of change. This has been the central problem of the Brazilian left. Banks, big business, most politicians, and most of the media lean to the right, yet the prevailing perception is that Brazil lives under a left-wing regime, and that the Bolsonaro camp is the alternative to the status quo. Lula has not managed to show that he, rather than the far right, represents change. That is partly because his administration has not been a government of change. Abstentions, blank votes, and spoiled ballots together reached 24 percent of the electorate. The rate of abstention alone was 21 percent, the highest since 1998. For the PT to win over even some former right-wing and anti-regime voters, and to build a social base of its own instead of watching it abstain, it will need a more combative strategy built on popular and social mobilization. That is the only way to defeat the far right. articles.title: Richie Floyd: Bernie’s 2016 Campaign Changed My Life
articles.author: Richie Floyd
articles.content: Bernie Sanders changed my life. And it happened overnight. Just over ten years ago, I was working as a hardware engineer. I grew up working class in the deeply conservative Florida Panhandle, where the Democratic Party had next to no foothold. The neoliberal ideas leading the conversation in the Democratic and Republican parties left me feeling disillusioned and unmoored from both the Left and the Right. I didn’t believe politics as it existed could have much of a positive impact on my life. While visiting with family at my parents’ house, I was asked by a friend if I had heard of Bernie Sanders. I had not, so he queued up a YouTube video called “Progress” in which Bernie stood on a stage on the shore of Lake Champlain in Burlington and outlined the major themes of his presidential campaign. I listened as he talked about universal health care, ending forever wars, getting money out of politics, and more. He clearly laid out the problems afflicting working-class Americans and named the enemy by saying, “This campaign is going to send a message to the billionaire class: You can’t have it all!” Never before had I seen my values reflected in a program in American politics. I was hooked. A Socialist City Councilor in Florida In the years that followed, I helped found my local Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) chapter, where I and many other Bernie supporters came together to organize. We gained valuable skills running campaigns like “DSA for Bernie” supporting Bernie’s 2020 presidential campaign, and campaigning for ballot initiatives like Amendment 2 in 2020 that raised the minimum wage to $15 an hour in Florida. We hosted reading groups and other educational events that deepened our analysis of local and national conditions. Discussions about the history of the labor movement and the importance of rank-and-file labor organizing ultimately led to my decision to leave engineering and become a union public-school teacher. Following the 2020 election, our DSA chapter began to search for candidates to compete in local elections, and — after a good bit of cajoling from comrades — I agreed to run for St Petersburg City Council in 2021. We built off the organizing lessons learned over the previous few years and set out to run a campaign funded by small-dollar donors and an army of door knockers, like the Bernie campaigns. We focused on local policy demands that would empower working people like social housing, protecting tenants’ and workers’ rights, and fighting for environmental justice. We built momentum over the course of the campaign and ended with more than 30,000 doors knocked, and over 2,000 individual contributions averaging right around $27 — again, just like Bernie’s campaigns. We ultimately received over 30,000 votes and defeated a former councilmember in a citywide race. I became the youngest person ever elected to St Petersburg City Council and the first openly socialist elected official in Florida in over a century. Since getting elected, I’ve worked in collaboration with my DSA chapter, labor unions, and other progressive organizations to enact an agenda that centers the working people of our city. When pandemic housing inflation hit Florida, we fought for rent control, legal aid for tenants, and money for affordable housing projects. Because of our organizing, we won a program that provides legal aid to every tenant in the city that faces eviction, and we spent more money from the American Rescue Plan on affordable housing than any other city in Florida. Since then, we’ve successfully won funding for local initiatives like street safety and public arts, and we’ve put forward resolutions speaking out on national issues like abortion rights and a ceasefire in Gaza. More recently, in 2024 I took an active role in another DSA member’s campaign for city council. Unfortunately, we came up just a few hundred votes short in the most conservative district in the city, but we learned valuable lessons through the process and trained new leaders in our chapter. Those leaders are now key to our campaign for the city to drop its investor-owned energy utility and move to public power. This summer, we successfully pushed the council to support my proposal to fund a feasibility study for the transition. And this year, I was reelected unopposed after launching another grassroots campaign that knocked on thousands of doors and collected hundreds of donations — more than any other campaign in the city — in just a few short months. Bernie’s Legacy None of this would have happened if not for Bernie’s first presidential campaign. I and so many of the leaders on our organizing campaigns had never contemplated democratic socialist politics before Bernie brought it into the mainstream over a decade ago. Many of DSA’s newest members are too young to remember much of that first campaign, but they often have stories similar to mine about their first exposure to other socialist candidates: like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Zohran Mamdani, or Oliver Larkin in Florida, who all worked on or volunteered for Bernie’s presidential campaigns themselves. It’s clear that the modern democratic socialist movement began on that lakefront in Burlington in 2015. Much has changed since then. Two terms of Donald Trump as president have led to crisis after crisis, unchecked militarism from both parties has disillusioned large swaths of the electorate, and an explosion in the cost of living has left working people struggling to stay afloat. These factors have driven people to the socialist movement as well, and for those of us who joined thanks to electoral campaigns, recent crises have helped drive home the point that our organizing must go beyond the ballot box. Still, nothing we do captures the attention of the public like high-profile socialist electoral campaigns. Continuing to elect DSA members to office will be crucial, and we can’t shy away from opportunities at attention-grabbing runs for executive office at the local, state, or even national level. Fortunately, we don’t have to start from scratch; we can begin by looking at the lessons learned during Bernie’s time as mayor of Burlington . Bernie’s insistence that the world can get better — and that working people are the ones who can make that happen — ignited a movement that gives me hope for the future. His campaign changed my life. In time, I believe the socialist movement that it reinvigorated will change our world. articles.title: Thomas Piketty’s Utopian Socialism
articles.author: Virgilio Urbina Lazardi
articles.content: In June, the policy world held its collective breath as the World Inequality Lab, the outfit headed by Thomas Piketty , released a report meant to serve as a capstone to years of extensive research on the elusive goal of leveling global incomes. Christened the Global Justice Report ( GJR ), Piketty and his collaborators promoted it as the first data-driven synthesis of two long-standing progressive ambitions that had remained more aspirational than actionable: dramatically reducing income and wealth inequality both within countries and between them, on the one hand, and achieving planetary sustainability in the age of global warming, on the other. The GJR , in short, aimed to demonstrate that the sort of inequality studies that had made Piketty famous with the 2013 publication of Capital in the Twenty-First Century could be used to navigate the trade-offs posed by the climate crisis. At first glance, there is much in the report with which socialists would agree. It envisions, to borrow John Maynard Keynes’s phrase, the euthanasia of the billionaire class within a quarter century, primarily through confiscatory taxation. It proposes to democratize institutions of international economic governance, long dominated by the same cadre of rich nations, by implementing a per capita voting formula and introducing an international currency that would mitigate the exorbitant privilege of the dollar. And as part of its overarching concern for planetary limits, it calls for a drastic shift in the translation of productivity gains away from ever-greater material output and toward more leisure time . This has been a long-standing socialist demand, one that capitalism’s drive for profit has delivered on fitfully and only under sustained pressure from below. Yet when it turns from the highlights to the machinery meant to achieve them, the report falls short. Far from an ambitious but feasible program that could be selectively used to rally the global left, the GJR retreats into the realm of fantastical thinking. Piketty and his collaborators passingly acknowledge the political constraints on building lasting coalitions of the dispossessed but ultimately sidestep them. Not unlike the schemes of the utopian socialists of the nineteenth century, the GJR flounders on the same obstacle: its proposals cannot cobble together a political constituency powerful enough to overcome the fierce resistance they would inevitably provoke from entrenched elites. Briefly stated, the GJR sets out a pathway to global income convergence by the end of the century that at the same time limits greenhouse gas emissions to two degrees Celsius above the preindustrial threshold. It employs a novel input-output accounting model to simulate warming pathways and adds a redistributive dimension that narrows the range of acceptable scenarios. The working papers that form the basis of the report reveal this to essentially consist of one long and complex accounting exercise. The input-output model first generates a maximum bank of future greenhouse gas emissions that the global economy can emit to remain within the two-degree target. It subsequently affixes a per capita income level that all countries could converge on that would respect this limit. Economic growth, both quantitative and qualitative, is thereby apportioned to each country based on a country-specific carbon footprint that the model determines would not run afoul of either goal of sustainability or equality. Once the apportionment is complete, the model backs out of the climate- and growth-enhancing investment shortfall that would be necessary to set the world’s economies on the path to sustainable equality. Enter the GJR ’s flagship proposal: the establishment of a mammoth Global Justice Fund with fiscal jurisdiction over the entire planet. After all is said and done, the GJR ’s model ascertains that the world can converge on a per capita income of €60,000 in the year 2100 while keeping warming to only 1.8 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels. The poorest regions of the world, such as sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, would grow at a blistering rate of 3 to 4 percent per year, whereas the Global North in its entirety would only be permitted a growth rate of 0 to 0.5 percent per year. Much, if not most, of that growth would be oriented toward so-called immaterial sectors, especially health and education. Quotas, among other consumption-shaping policy instruments, would keep a lid on spending on material sectors. The investment shortfall to achieve this level of convergence would equal approximately 10 percent of world GDP each year. The end point is set; the trajectory is mapped out — but how do we get there? Enter the GJR ’s flagship proposal: the establishment of a mammoth Global Justice Fund (GJF) with fiscal jurisdiction over the entire planet. Through confiscatory income and wealth tax schedules, targeted almost exclusively at the global top 1 percent, the fund would raise the investment needed to finance the transition through the late 2050s. By then, the report projects, the world’s billionaire class would have effectively disappeared, and enough revenue would have been accumulated in the proposed World Sovereign Fund (WSF) for future spending to become self-financing. The rest of the story is straightforward. The GJF and the WSF would distribute their investments and dividends to nations according to the growth targets of the model, in the process providing incentives for countries to come up with projects that not only are climate-friendly — by expanding relatively immaterial sectors and reducing working hours — but also advance broad social goals, such as flattening gender differences in working hours and experimenting with communal or other alternative forms of property ownership. To prevent rich countries from dominating the system, the report proposes that the fund operate on a double-majority vote formula based on country population rather than the GDP-weighted one used today in institutions like the International Monetary Fund. It also calls for the United Nations to issue a new global currency, eliminating any single coalition’s disproportionate influence over the financial infrastructure of global trade. Most criticism of the report has focused on the staggering collective action problems that the requirement of universal or near-universal participation in the GJF introduces. Indeed, in an anarchic world-system beset by the security dilemma, it is hard to imagine that enough rich or upper-middle-income countries would willingly give up a significant fraction of their tax authority and revenues for the project to even get off the ground. The example of the European Union, which, unlike the GJF, does not have to aggregate such disparate national interests as those of Laos and Canada, is sobering in this regard. Seventy-five years after starting the process of economic integration, the EU lacks anything resembling the fiscal union (or capital market integration) that the GJF would require of the entire world. On the other side of the ledger, poor countries have an incentive to free ride on the emissions reduction efforts undertaken by their wealthier peers while ignoring the GJF’s strictures. The report’s authors offer the use of punitive tariffs and other economic sanctions to keep nonparticipants in line, but this simply reintroduces the obstacle in another guise. If the GJF cannot solicit the participation of the world’s most powerful countries with the deepest tax bases in the first place, with what authority could it credibly threaten to impose penalties on them? Daunting as the challenge of corralling today’s heavily armed sovereign states without a world Leviathan may be, the critics still understate the severity of the problem by stopping there. It ought to go without saying that any movement toward the implementation of the GJF would solicit maximal resistance on the part of economic elites. No period in modern history has come remotely close to approximating the scale of downward wealth redistribution — within or between countries — that the fund proposes to accomplish in a mere handful of decades. This alone undermines the report’s repeated insistence that its projections are consistent with historical precedent, whether referring to the rapid growth of the Asian Tigers from the 1970s through the 2010s or the compression of incomes in the Nordic countries between the 1930s and the 1980s. More than two centuries of political experimentation have shown that capitalists have only been durably constrained by the unlikely, difficult, and fragile organizing of the laboring masses around shared material interests, not altruism. And it is here that the report digs its own grave by ignoring the legitimate concerns of workers in the Global North. As stated above, the report’s model awards developed countries near-zero yearly growth for the remainder of the century. Aware of the damaging political implications that might flow from this, the report engages in what can only be described as an intellectually dishonest sleight of hand by positing that, when factoring in the compression of incomes, most of the inhabitants of the Global North (specifically, the bottom four-fifths of the income distribution) would nonetheless experience a doubling of their monetary incomes between now and 2100. In fact, this represents a ceiling on income growth that most Northern workers wouldn’t come close to experiencing, although the bottom 20 percent could experience something slightly above it. The implicit claim seems to be that because this does not constitute a net reduction in incomes, the political allegiance of most of the North’s population would not be seriously jeopardized. But as the World Inequality Lab’s economists surely know, the reality of modern growth is such that sustained income losses — outside of economic depressions — are a rare experience. The question is, rather, how fast incomes grow. And a doubling of incomes in seventy-five years represents an annual growth rate of less than 1 percent, which, incidentally, has been the rate of growth of median household incomes during the neoliberal period . In other words, in the report’s ideal scenario, the workers of the developed world would be subjected to the near-austerity conditions of the last thirty years until at least the end of the century, if not beyond. This objection does not rest on any chauvinistic preference for the welfare of Northern workers, although it should raise some alarm bells that a growing coterie of progressive thinkers now seem to think it’s acceptable to deny up to one-fifth of the world’s population most of the benefits of economic growth. It is instead a sober-minded exercise in strategic thinking. Regardless of one’s judgment on the moral worthiness of these workers, the inescapable reality is that securing their participation in a cross-country redistributive scheme is not at all optional. Due to Northern workers’ structural position within the most productive economies of the planet, in addition to their ability to exercise the political rights they have won through centuries of struggle, they and they alone hold the leverage to inflict the sort of penalties on Northern capital that would be necessary to inaugurate a fairer global dispensation. Yet what the GJR proposes is that workers in the advanced capitalist world shoulder the Herculean task of reversing decades of tax cuts for the rich, only to hand over most of the resulting gains to a distant tax authority that has already determined in advance that they have had enough. If there is a central political lesson to be taken from the rise of the far right in the last decade, it is that the more a political fight is framed as — or resembles — a zero-sum game between workers, the more they will turn aside from universalistic appeals in favor of exclusionary ones. This response flows directly from the insecurity inherent to the proletarian condition. In this sense, the GJR represents an unintentional ideological gift to the nationalist right, even as it purports to endorse a class-based appeal in its concluding sections. Of course, the report’s authors would regard all this as beside the point, since their selective embrace of degrowth is, according to their input-output model, the only path consistent with limiting warming to two degrees. Their actual tone, however, is considerably more caustic. In a revealing reply to a Financial Times columnist, they argue that the view that “current generations [in the North] should not be [held] responsible for their ancestors’ actions. . . . rests on shaky ground.” So much for that class-based appeal. It may come as a surprise, then, that one searches in vain for any serious engagement in the report or its working papers with the burgeoning climate economics literature on the decoupling of growth from material throughput, including but by no means limited to greenhouse gas emissions. The report treats the decoupling phenomenon as settled science instead of a live debate, quickly disposing of it through selective citation of its most bad-faith critics. Ironically, it is precisely the environmentalist movement’s partial but genuine successes in the Global North that have already placed a growing number of countries on a decoupling trajectory for more than two decades, even after accounting for the material footprint of imports. While decoupling is not yet occurring at the pace required to avoid the worst of the climate crisis, a plausible alternative to degrowth has nonetheless been taking shape before our eyes. That fact makes the report’s insistence on an exceedingly pessimistic extrapolation of current trends all the more perplexing, including the use in its input-output model of assumptions seemingly lifted from the worst-case RCP8.5 scenario that was recently retired by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. More could be said about the report’s proclivity toward excessive centralization. This is most visible in the unwieldy structure of the GJF, which in its governance comes uncomfortably close to the Right’s much-ballyhooed nightmare of a globalist technocracy — one that intrusively delimits how ordinary people far removed from its halls can shape their own future. Once again, the experience of the European Union, which has been roiled by one crisis of legitimacy after another, is instructive here. However, in the end, the GJR will almost certainly disappear without a trace into the capacious graveyard of well-intentioned policy briefs for one very simple reason: its inability to mobilize majoritarian political constituencies where it matters most. This should not be cause for smarmy celebration but rather painful disappointment. Aside from their many invaluable contributions to the study of economic inequality, the intellectual trajectory of Piketty and the World Inequality Lab since the publication of Capital in the Twenty-First Century has been one of the most encouraging developments in contemporary academia. Starting off as relatively conventional social democratic researchers, their analysis came to resemble the socialist left’s class-struggle perspective , centered on the need to rebuild the working-class institutions with proven track records of wresting wealth, power, and influence away from elites. A quick comparison of the role of trade unions in the explanatory apparatus of Capital in the Twenty-First Century with that presented in Piketty’s 2019 follow-up, Capital and Ideology , makes this shift unmistakable. Considering the vast amount of time and resources spent by the World Inequality Lab on putting together the GJR , however, it seems clear that much of that progress has been undone. More than a decade ago, Jacobin held a symposium on Piketty’s work that (fairly) accused him of putting forward policy platforms so devoid of a realistic assessment of the balance of class forces as to make him “a general without an army.” Sadly, the same charge is even more appropriate for this latest venture.
